body: Grasslands, savannas and open woodlands of sub-Saharan Africa, with a small population in India's Gir Forest.
Lions are the only truly social big cats, living in prides where related females do most of the hunting.
A lion's roar can be heard up to 8 km away.
Tropical rainforests, mangrove swamps, grasslands and snowy taiga across South and East Asia.
No two tigers have the same stripe pattern, and the stripes are on their skin as well as their fur.
Fewer than 6,000 tigers remain in the wild, but numbers have been rising thanks to protection efforts in India and Nepal.
The most widespread wild cat, found from African rainforests and deserts to the mountains of Asia.
Leopards often haul prey heavier than themselves up into trees to keep it away from lions and hyenas.
Rainforests, wetlands and grasslands of Central and South America, with the Pantanal a major stronghold.
Jaguars have one of the strongest bites of any cat relative to size and often kill by biting straight through the skull.
Open grasslands and savannas of eastern and southern Africa, plus a tiny critically endangered population in Iran.
The fastest land animal, reaching around 100 km/h in short sprints of a few hundred metres.
Cheetahs cannot roar. Instead they chirp, purr and make bird-like yelps.
High, rocky mountain ranges of Central Asia, including the Himalayas, usually 3,000-4,500 m above sea level.
They wrap their long, thick tails around their faces like a scarf to stay warm.
Forests, tundra, deserts and grasslands across North America, Europe and Asia.
Wolves live in family packs and can travel over 50 km in a single day while hunting.
Forests, mountains and tundra across North America, Europe and northern Asia.
A brown bear's sense of smell is thought to be thousands of times better than a human's.
Arctic sea ice and coastlines, where it hunts seals from the edge of the ice.
Polar bear fur is actually transparent and their skin is black, which helps absorb heat.
Melting sea ice from climate change is the biggest threat, as bears rely on it to hunt seals.
Savannas, forests, deserts and marshes across sub-Saharan Africa.
The largest living land animal. A bull can weigh over 6 tonnes.
Elephants can detect rumbling calls from other elephants several kilometres away, partly through their feet.
Rivers, lakes and swamps of sub-Saharan Africa, resting in water by day and grazing on land at night.
Hippos secrete a red, oily fluid sometimes called 'blood sweat' that acts as a natural sunscreen.
Grassland and savanna of southern and eastern Africa.
Southern white rhinos were reduced to fewer than 100 animals around 1900 and recovered to thousands thanks to protection.
Lowland tropical rainforests and swamps of west-central Africa.
Gorillas build a fresh nest of leaves and branches to sleep in every night.
Tropical forests and wooded savannas of central and west Africa.
Chimpanzees make and use tools, such as stripping twigs to fish termites out of mounds.
Every ocean in the world, from polar seas to the tropics.
Orcas are actually the largest member of the dolphin family, and different pods have their own hunting techniques and 'dialects'.
All the world's oceans, migrating between cold feeding waters and warmer breeding grounds.
The largest animal known to have ever lived, bigger than any dinosaur. Its heart is the size of a small car.
Warm and temperate seas worldwide, from coastal bays to the open ocean.
Each dolphin develops its own signature whistle that works like a name.
Dry savannas, deserts and forests across Africa, the Middle East and India.
Its thick, loose skin lets it twist round and bite back even when grabbed by a predator.
Remote boreal forests, tundra and mountains of the far north.
Despite their size, wolverines have been seen driving bears and wolves away from carcasses.
Savannas, grasslands, woodlands and semi-deserts of sub-Saharan Africa.
Spotted hyenas are skilled hunters that catch most of their own food, not just scavengers.
The most widespread wild carnivore, living everywhere from Arctic tundra to city centres.
Red foxes may use Earth's magnetic field to aim their pounces on mice hidden under snow.
Savannas and open woodlands of sub-Saharan Africa.
The tallest land animal. Adults can be over 5.5 m tall.
A giraffe's tongue can be around 45-50 cm long and is dark coloured, possibly to prevent sunburn.
Savannas, swamps and forests across sub-Saharan Africa.
Herds will gang up to defend members from lions, and buffalo kill several lions every year.
Boreal and mixed forests of North America, northern Europe and Asia.
Moose are excellent swimmers and can dive several metres to eat underwater plants.
Dry grasslands and deserts of mainland Australia.
The largest living marsupial. It can cover around 8 m in a single bound.
Freshwater rivers and streams of eastern Australia and Tasmania.
One of the only mammals that lays eggs. It hunts with its eyes closed using electroreceptors in its bill.
Male platypuses have a venomous spur on their hind legs.
Tropical and subtropical regions of Central and South America.
Vampire bats share blood meals with roost-mates who failed to feed, and remember who has helped them.
Tropical rainforests of Central and South America.
Algae grow on their fur, giving them a green tint that helps them hide in the canopy.
Savannas and woodlands of eastern and southern Africa.
Pangolins are thought to be the most trafficked wild mammals in the world, hunted for their scales and meat.
Their scales are made of keratin, the same material as human fingernails.
Grasslands, forests and scrub from South America to the southern United States.
Females almost always give birth to identical quadruplets from a single egg.
Woodlands, grasslands and suburbs across North America.
A skunk can spray its foul-smelling musk accurately up to about 3 m.
Forests, marshes and cities across North America, and introduced to Europe and Japan.
Raccoons have extremely sensitive front paws and can solve complex locks.
Forests and coastal scrub of Tasmania.
The largest living carnivorous marsupial, with one of the strongest bites for its size of any mammal.
A contagious facial tumour disease has wiped out a large share of the wild population since the 1990s.
Arctic seas around the North Pole, resting on sea ice and beaches.
Walruses use their tusks to haul themselves out of the water onto ice.
Coastal waters of the northern Pacific, especially kelp forests.
Sea otters use rocks as tools to crack open shellfish, and they hold hands while sleeping so they don't drift apart.
Open grasslands and deserts of western North America.
The fastest land animal in the Americas, able to sustain high speeds much longer than a cheetah.
Every continent except Antarctica, from cliffs and coasts to city skyscrapers.
The fastest animal on Earth. In a hunting dive (stoop) it has been measured at over 320 km/h.
Pesticides like DDT nearly wiped them out in the 20th century. Banning DDT allowed a remarkable recovery.
Mountains, cliffs and open country across the Northern Hemisphere.
Golden eagles have been known to hunt prey as large as young deer.
Lowland tropical rainforests of Central and South America.
Its rear talons can be up to 13 cm long, longer than a grizzly bear's claws.
Forests, deserts, swamps and cities from the Arctic to South America.
Great horned owls have a very poor sense of smell, so they regularly hunt skunks.
Farmland, grassland and open countryside on every continent except Antarctica.
Barn owls can catch mice in complete darkness using hearing alone.
Savannas and semi-deserts of Africa.
The largest living bird and the fastest on land. It lays the largest eggs of any living bird.
Tropical rainforests of New Guinea and north-eastern Australia.
The inner toe of each foot has a dagger-like claw up to 12 cm long.
Sea ice and the cold waters surrounding Antarctica.
The deepest-diving bird, recorded at over 500 m below the surface.
Forests, mountains, deserts and coasts across the Northern Hemisphere.
Ravens can plan for the future, solve multi-step puzzles and even mimic human speech.
Lowland rainforests of west and central Africa.
Grey parrots can learn hundreds of words and use some of them in the right context.
Huge numbers were taken from the wild for the pet trade, which is now banned internationally.
Woodlands and gardens of eastern North America, migrating to Central America for winter.
Its wings beat around 50 times per second, and it flies non-stop across the Gulf of Mexico on migration.
The open Southern Ocean, nesting on sub-Antarctic islands.
The largest wingspan of any living bird, reaching around 3.5 m.
Open grasslands and savannas of sub-Saharan Africa.
It hunts snakes by stamping on them with powerful, rapid kicks.
Freshwater swamps of central and eastern Africa.
Shoebills can stand completely still for long periods while waiting to ambush lungfish.
Breeds across Europe and Asia, wintering in sub-Saharan Africa.
Swifts can stay airborne for around 10 months at a time, eating and even sleeping on the wing.
The Andes mountains and Pacific coasts of South America.
One of the heaviest flying birds. It can soar for hours, sometimes flapping only about 1% of the time.
Coastal rivers, estuaries and mangroves from India to northern Australia, and sometimes the open sea.
The largest living reptile, with the strongest bite ever directly measured in an animal.
Rivers, lakes and marshes across sub-Saharan Africa.
Nile crocodiles may wait for weeks at river crossings used by migrating wildebeest.
Dry grasslands and forests on a handful of Indonesian islands, including Komodo.
The largest living lizard. It has venom glands in its lower jaw.
Rainforests and mangroves of South and Southeast Asia.
The longest venomous snake in the world. It mostly eats other snakes.
Savannas, rocky hills and woodlands of eastern and southern Africa.
Black mambas are actually grey or brown. Their name comes from the inky black inside of their mouth.
Swamps, marshes and slow rivers of the Amazon and Orinoco basins.
The heaviest snake in the world.
Rainforests, woodlands and grasslands of Southeast Asia.
The longest snake in the world, with records of over 6 m.
Dry floodplains and cracking clay soils of central eastern Australia.
It has the most toxic venom of any land snake, but it is shy and bites to humans are very rare.
The Galapagos Islands, from dry lowlands to humid highlands.
Among the longest-lived vertebrates, with lifespans of over 100 years.
Open oceans worldwide, from the tropics to sub-polar seas.
The largest living turtle, and it dives deeper than 1,000 m to hunt jellyfish.
Rivers, lakes and swamps of the south-eastern United States.
It lures fish into its open mouth by wiggling a worm-shaped pink appendage on its tongue.
Rainforests and scrub of Madagascar.
Its eyes move independently, giving it almost 360-degree vision, and its tongue can shoot out longer than its body.
Deserts of the south-western United States and north-western Mexico.
A compound from Gila monster saliva led to a medicine used to treat type 2 diabetes.
Rainforests on the Pacific coast of Colombia.
One of the most poisonous animals on Earth. Its toxins come from its wild diet, so captive-bred frogs are harmless.
Only the lake and canal system of Xochimilco near Mexico City.
Axolotls can regrow lost limbs, parts of their heart and even parts of their brain.
Although common in aquariums, wild axolotls are critically endangered due to pollution and urban growth.
Cool, fast-flowing mountain streams in China.
The largest amphibian in the world, reaching up to 1.8 m long.
Native to Central and South America, and invasive across northern and eastern Australia.
Introduced to Australia in 1935 to control beetles, cane toads became a major invasive species that poisons native predators.
Cool coastal waters worldwide, especially around South Africa, Australia and California.
Great whites can sense tiny electric fields from prey using organs called ampullae of Lorenzini.
Tropical and warm temperate seas worldwide.
Known as the 'garbage can of the sea', tiger sharks have been found with licence plates and tyres in their stomachs.
Tropical coastal waters and coral reefs worldwide.
Its wide head spreads out its sensors, helping it find stingrays buried in sand.
Warm tropical oceans worldwide.
The largest fish in the world, yet it feeds on tiny plankton.
Tropical and subtropical oceans worldwide, often near coastlines and reefs.
Mantas have the largest brain-to-body ratio of any fish and may recognise themselves in a mirror.
Warm waters of the Indian and Pacific oceans.
Sailfish are often called the fastest fish at around 110 km/h, but recent studies suggest a more modest figure. Scientists are still debating it.
The Atlantic Ocean and Mediterranean Sea.
Unlike most fish, bluefin tuna are warm-blooded, keeping their muscles warmer than the surrounding water.
Rivers and floodplains of the Amazon basin in South America.
Piranhas are mostly scavengers and often form shoals to protect themselves from predators.
Murky rivers and swamps of the Amazon and Orinoco basins.
It can produce shocks of around 600-860 volts. It is not a true eel but a type of knifefish.
Shallow coral reefs and rocky areas of the Indo-Pacific.
The most venomous fish in the world, with 13 venomous spines along its back.
Temperate and tropical oceans worldwide.
The heaviest bony fish in the world. A female can produce around 300 million eggs at once.
Rivers, lakes and bayous of the south-eastern United States and Mexico.
A 'living fossil' whose ancestors date back around 100 million years. Its armour-like scales were once used as arrowheads.
Lowland rainforests of Central and South America.
Its sting is considered among the most painful of any insect, said to feel like being shot.
Forests and mountains of East Asia.
Japanese honey bees defend against it by surrounding the hornet and vibrating to cook it with body heat.
Grasslands and gardens of East Asia, introduced to North America.
Mantises can turn their heads 180 degrees to look over their shoulders.
Rainforests of Central and South America and the Lesser Antilles.
One of the longest beetles in the world, with males reaching 17 cm including the horn.
Ponds, lakes and slow rivers across Europe, Africa and Asia.
Dragonflies are among the most successful hunters on Earth, catching prey in up to 95% of attempts.
Deserts and dry grasslands of Africa, the Middle East and South Asia.
Swarms can contain billions of locusts and eat as much food in a day as millions of people.
Meadows and fields across North America, migrating to Mexico and California for winter.
Some monarchs migrate up to 4,000 km, a journey no single butterfly makes twice.
Native to Europe, Africa and the Middle East, now kept worldwide.
Honey bees perform a 'waggle dance' to tell hive-mates the direction and distance to flowers.
Grasslands and woodlands of Europe.
It defends itself by mixing chemicals to fire a boiling-hot spray from its rear end.
Little Barrier Island (Hauturu) in New Zealand.
One of the heaviest insects ever recorded, at around 70 g, heavier than a sparrow.
Rainforests of Southeast Asia.
It looks like a flower and can attract pollinating insects even better than real flowers.
Found worldwide wherever cats and dogs live.
Fleas can jump over 100 times their own body length.
Rainforest floors of northern South America.
The largest spider in the world by mass. Despite the name, it rarely eats birds.
Woodpiles, sheds and sheltered places across the south-eastern United States.
Its silk is incredibly strong for its weight and has been studied for use in materials science.
Deserts and dry scrub of North Africa and the Middle East.
Like all scorpions, it glows blue-green under ultraviolet light.
Woodlands and scrub of the south-eastern United States and the Caribbean.
Jumping spiders have some of the sharpest vision of any invertebrate and can plan detours to reach prey.
Forests and suburbs within about 100 km of Sydney, Australia.
No one has died from a funnel-web bite since antivenom was introduced in 1981, thanks partly to spiders donated by the public.
Coastal waters of the northern Pacific Ocean.
Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood, and can change colour and texture in a fraction of a second.
Coral reefs and tide pools of the western Pacific and Indian oceans.
Though golf-ball sized, it carries tetrodotoxin, one of the most powerful toxins in nature.
Coral reefs of the Indo-Pacific.
Its club-like arms punch at around 80 km/h, fast enough to boil the water around them and crack aquarium glass.
Islands of the Indian and Pacific oceans.
The largest land-living arthropod, with a pinch as strong as the bite of many predators.
Coastal waters of northern Australia and the Indo-Pacific.
Box jellyfish have 24 eyes, and some of them can form images.
Rainforests and caves of northern South America and the Caribbean.
Some hang from cave ceilings to catch bats in mid-air.
